table.text: Approval was also obtained from the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics Midt-Norge for the HUNT study (REK-656785) and the Coordinating Ethical Committee of the Helsinki and Uusimaa University Hospital District for the FINRISK cohort (558/E3/2001).
All studies were conducted according to principles laid out in the Declaration of Helsinki.

The Swedish Ethical Review Authority has approved the conduct of the present study (DNR 2022-06137-01 with amendments 2023-04785-02, 2024-05416-02, and 2025-03082-02) and all included participants have provided informed consent.

The Swedish CArdioPulmonary BioImage Study (SCAPIS) aimed to improve understanding and prediction of cardiopulmonary diseases, and its design has been previously described. 16 The participants were invited based on a random selection from the population register in six areas adjacent to six university hospitals across Sweden 2014-2018 (50% participation rate).

table.text: The participants were asked to collect fecal samples after the first visit and store them at home (-20°C) until the second visit to the study site, after which the samples were stored at -80°C. The present study included participants who were not part of the SCAPIS cohort.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Variation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs.
We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality.

We assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS).

Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing.
Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK.
Results: During a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred.
Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95).

Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in ≥30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus.
Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales, an order in which butyrate production has been reported.

Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health.
Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans.
No associations were observed with ischemic stroke.

Conclusions: Gut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

The gut microbiome, a collection of microbes living in the gastrointestinal tract that plays important roles in human physiological processes, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] Proposed mechanisms for the role of the gut microbiome in ASCVD pathophysiology include the production of microbial-derived metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and secondary bile acids, which are involved in lipid metabolism and immune signaling. 1, 2 Detection of bacterial DNA and biofilms of the oral pathogen Streptococcus in coronary plaques suggests an additional mechanism specific to oral bacteria.

text.text: The three primary outcomes were 1) incident total ASCVD, which included IHD and ischemic stroke events, and separately, 2) incident IHD, or 3) incident ischemic stroke.
Information about ASCVD events was obtained through linkage to the Swedish National Patient Register and the Cause of Death Register.
Individuals with prevalent ASCVD at baseline were identified and excluded from all association analyses.
IHD included non-fatal and fatal IHD.

Non-fatal IHD included ICD-10 codes I21-I22 or ICD-9 410 as main diagnoses, or coronary procedures such as percutaneous coronary intervention and coronary artery bypass graft surgery (Nordic surgery codes FNG02, FNG05, FNC, FND, and FNE).
Fatal IHD included deaths coded as I20-I25 as the underlying cause of death.
Ischemic stroke was defined as events with ICD-10 I63 or ICD-9 433-434 as main diagnosis or underlying cause of death.
For analysis with total ASCVD as the outcome, only the first occurrence of either IHD or ischemic stroke was considered.

Follow-up time was calculated for each individual from the date of fecal sampling (for SIMPLER) or screening date (for SCAPIS and MOS) until the date of incident event, death, emigration date, or the end of follow-up, whichever came first.
The end of follow-up was 31 December 2022 for SIMPLER, 31 December 2023 for MOS, and 30 September 2024 for SCAPIS.
Covariates are harmonized across discovery cohorts when possible; expanded information is provided in the Supplementary Methods.
Information on age and sex was derived from the Swedish Population Register.
Education and physical activity level were self-reported by using questionnaires.
Education level was categorized into ≤9 years, 10-12 years, and >12 years.
text.formatted: Education level was categorized into ≤9 years, 10-12 years, and >12 years.

text.text: Physical activity was limited to leisure time, with cohort-specific categories.

Birth country, based on questionnaire responses or linkage to the Swedish Tax Register, was categorized in SIMPLER and SCAPIS into Sweden, Europe other than Sweden, and others, and in MOS as Sweden or others.
Smoking status was categorized into current, former, or never smokers.

Data on usual dietary intakes were collected at the same time as fecal sampling, using validated food frequency questionnaires in SCAPIS 23 and SIMPLER, 24 or a 4-d web-based food record in MOS, 25 and nutrient intakes were obtained by linkage to the Swedish food composition database.
text.formatted: Data on usual dietary intakes were collected at the same time as fecal sampling, using validated food frequency questionnaires in SCAPIS <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">23</ref> and SIMPLER, <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">24</ref> or a 4-d web-based food record in MOS, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">25</ref> and nutrient intakes were obtained by linkage to the Swedish food composition database.

text.text: Information on medication use across all cohorts was obtained primarily through linkage to the National Prescribed Drug Register and was additionally confirmed by questionnaire or detected drug metabolites in blood when available.

During visits to study centers, participants underwent anthropometric measurements including height (in cm) and weight (in kg), from which body mass index (BMI, kg/m 2 ) was calculated, and waist circumference (in cm).
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure were measured twice, and the average of the two measurements was used.
Venous blood samples were collected (non-fasted samples <1% in SCAPIS).
text.formatted: Venous blood samples were collected (non-fasted samples <1% in SCAPIS).

text.text: Fresh plasma samples were used to measure glucose (mmol/L) with the enzymatic method with hexokinase, lipids (total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol (HDL-C), mmol/L), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP, mg/L) using the immunoturbidimetric method, and creatinine (µmol/L) with the enzymatic colorimetric method.
LDL cholesterol (LDL-C, mmol/L) was directly measured or calculated using Friedewald's formula.

EDTA-plasma samples were used to measure apolipoprotein B (ApoB), lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), cystatin C (mg/L), and liver enzymes aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT, µkat/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALAT, µkat/L), gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT, µkat/L).
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated using the CKD-EPI 2021 formula using both creatinine and cystatin C. 26

text.text: The EDTA plasma samples were analyzed in three different batches: Malmö (n=3,720), Uppsala-1 (n=2,825), Uppsala-2, (n=1,855).

Untargeted ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) across four different platforms was used to measure the metabolites, which were subsequently identified by comparison with a reference standard library.
When the measured value was below the detection threshold, the next higher value was used to impute the measured value.

Data on dental procedures, diagnoses, and the number of teeth were obtained for 96% SCAPIS participants through linkage to data from the Swedish National Dental Health Register (during 2010-2020) and were processed to derive measures of periodontitis status, caries status, and the number of missing teeth.

The derivation and validation of these measures have been described in detail previously. 28, 29 Severe periodontitis status (present vs. absent) was defined by using records indicating a history of tooth extraction or surgical treatment (procedural codes starting with "4") due to periodontitis (condition "periodontitis") and two extensive sessions of nonsurgical periodontal treatment (procedural codes 342/343, along with the condition "periodontitis").

text.text: The Trøndelag Health Study (the HUNT study) is an ongoing population-based cohort comprising adults ≥20 y residing in Trøndelag county, Norway, and has recruited >200,000 participants since its start in 1984.

text.text: Between 2017 and 2019, the participants were invited to the HUNT4 survey, and 56,042 individuals were included. 30 Of these participants, 13,268 participants provided fecal samples for gut microbiome measurement.

text.text: For the replication analysis, microbiome data were available from 12,887 participants.
After excluding 2,736 participants with missing covariate data and 373 prevalent IHD cases, data from 9,778 participants were analyzed.
Median follow-up was 5.4 y.
Methods for gut microbiome measurement, outcome and covariate definition are further described in the Supplementary Methods.

The FINRISK cohort is a national cohort initiated in 1972 whose data collection was conducted every 5 years by the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare up to 2012. 31 The data used in this study were from the FINRISK 2002 cohort, which included 8,738 participants aged 25-74.

text.text: At the 2002 baseline, the participants completed questionnaires on sociodemographic and lifestyle factors, underwent health examinations, and donated fecal samples.

For the replication analysis, participants without fecal samples, with missing covariates or with prevalent IHD were excluded (total n excluded=1,722), resulting in data from 5,321 individuals, with a median follow-up of 17.8 y.
Methods for gut microbiome measurement and definition for the outcome and covariates are further described in the Supplementary Methods.
A base-2 logarithmic function was used to transform non-rarefied species relative abundance data after replacing zero values with half of the species-specific minimum value.

Cox proportional hazards models with age as the underlying timescale were used to estimate hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals (HR [95% CI]) for associations between gut microbial features and incident total ASCVD, IHD, and ischemic stroke, implemented using the survival R package (v.3.5-5).
Two analytical models were used.
The minimally adjusted model included sex, birth country, and a technical covariate (metagenomic extraction plate in SCAPIS and MOS, aliquoting plate in SIMPLER).

The fully adjusted model additionally included education level, smoking status, leisure time physical activity, energy-adjusted intakes of carbohydrate, polyunsaturated fatty acid, saturated fatty acid, and fiber, total energy intake, alcohol intake (not energy-adjusted), cardiovascular medication use, proton-pump inhibitor use, and prevalent diabetes.
To account for the relatedness among MOS participants, we added a frailty term to the Cox models for MOS data.
All covariates were specified a priori, and a directed acyclic graph was used to inform the adjustment sets (Supplementary Fig. 2).
text.formatted: All covariates were specified a priori, and a directed acyclic graph was used to inform the adjustment sets (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>).

text.text: To handle missing data in covariates, multiple imputation with ten imputed datasets was performed in each discovery cohort, and estimates from the imputed datasets were pooled using Rubin's rules; all implemented using the mice R package (v3.16.0).
Details for missing data handling were further expanded in Supplementary Methods.
All analyses were performed using RStudio v2023.12.1.402 (R v4.3.1), unless specified otherwise.

Cohort-specific estimates were meta-analyzed using a fixed-effects model with inversevariance weighting to estimate outcome-specific hazard ratios and 95% CIs for each microbiome feature (alpha diversity and metagenomic species).

Microbiome features were considered to be associated with the outcome in the meta-analysis when passing multiple testing correction using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate set at 5% (q<0.05).
text.formatted: Microbiome features were considered to be associated with the outcome in the meta-analysis when passing multiple testing correction using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate set at 5% (q<0.05).

text.text: For the outcome ischemic stroke which had much fewer events, we used the cut-off prevalence of 1.5%, and estimates from 75 species were meta-analyzed.
Meta-analyses were performed using the metafor R package (v4.8.0) in RStudio v2025.05.0+496 with R v4.5.2.
Sensitivity analyses were performed in each cohort, and results from each cohort were subsequently meta-analyzed.

We 1) further adjusted the results from the primary analyses (i.e., the fully adjusted model) for BMI, 2) excluded individuals receiving antibiotic treatment six months prior to fecal sampling, 3) excluded those with prevalent inflammatory bowel diseases, and 4) excluded the first two years of follow-up by starting the follow-up time two years after the fecal sampling to assess potential reverse causality.

For analysis of microbial species, we also 5) further adjusted the results for richness, 6) performed censoring after three years of follow-up, and 7) applied different types of transformations to relative abundance data (details in Supplementary Methods).

In SIMPLER, collection of fecal samples occurred over a longer time span relative to SCAPIS or MOS; we therefore also performed an additional sensitivity analysis to examine this effect by 8) including age-at-entry as a stratifying variable when fitting Cox regression on SIMPLER data.

We performed partial Spearman correlations for microbial features identified in the primary analyses with age, sex, birth country, adiposity (BMI, waist circumference), and clinical ASCVD risk factors when available in the cohort, including plasma glucose, lipids, hsCRP, and measures of kidney and liver function.
For age, sex, and birth country, correlations were adjusted for technical variation (plate).
For all other risk factors, Spearman's partial correlations were adjusted for age, sex, and technical variation.
Multiple testing adjustment was performed using a 5% false discovery rate per microbiome feature identified in the primary analyses.

We performed partial Spearman correlations between microbial features identified in the primary analyses and 1,326 plasma metabolites in the SCAPIS cohort (max n=8,400), adjusting for metabolomics delivery batch, metagenomic extraction plate, age, sex, and birth country.
We analyzed all metabolites detected in at least 100 samples.

For metabolites that were detected in <2% of the individuals or classified as drug metabolites (n=105), these were analyzed as binary variables (detected/not detected), with the exception of 2,6dihydroxybenzoic acid and salicylate (detected in >99% of the individuals).

text.text: The SIMPLER cohort comprised older individuals than those in SCAPIS and MOS; it also had fewer current smokers, and a higher proportion of individuals using cardiovascular medication and proton-pump inhibitors at the time of fecal sampling.

Individuals who developed IHD events during the follow-up were more often males, and at baseline, less likely to be never smokers or be physically active, had higher saturated fatty acid and lower fiber intakes, as compared to those who remained free from IHD.

Those who later experienced IHD events were also more likely to have diabetes and had a worse cardiovascular risk profile at baseline, despite also being more likely to be using cardiovascular medications (Supplementary Table 3).

text.text: We present a large prospective study assessing the association between the gut microbiome and incident ASCVD, including 17,216 community-dwelling participants with 769 ASCVD events over a median follow-up of 6-8 years.
We identified four bacterial species that were adversely associated with IHD after extensive adjustment for confounders, including the oral bacteria S. mutans and L. fermentum.
Furthermore, gut microbial diversity and five species were inversely associated with risk of IHD.

We found that the gut abundance of the oral species S. mutans and L. fermentum, known to be involved in dental caries when present in the mouth, was positively associated with IHD in the Swedish cohorts, with similar effect estimates in the HUNT study.

These findings corroborate our earlier cross-sectional analysis of the microbiome composition in relation to image-based measures of coronary atherosclerosis in SCAPIS. 12 Gut abundances of Streptococcus and other oral taxa have been repeatedly reported to be associated with prevalent cardiovascular disease, [34] [35] [36] [37] [38] [39] and in a recent prospective study with new-onset hypertension. 14 Oral disease has been associated with increased ASCVD risk, 28, 33 with proposed mechanisms including increased translocation of oral bacteria and/or bacterial components from the oral cavity to the gut and/or to circulation due to poor oral health, as well as modulation of local and systemic inflammation by the oral bacteria. 33, 40 It has also been suggested that an increased abundance of oral species in the gut is a marker for microbial imbalance ("dysbiosis") and depletion of commensal bacteria. 41 Our analysis strategy accounted for medications related to such depletion, and models adjusted for diversity showed virtually unchanged estimates, making this explanation less likely.

text.text: We observed an inverse association between gut microbial diversity and risk of IHD.

Previous evidence for an association of microbial diversity and ASCVD is conflicting; most case-control studies 6, 37, 38, 58 reported no associations, while a limited number of crosssectional analyses in individuals without prior CVD showed that microbial diversity was inversely associated with CVD risk score 59, 60 and with subclinical atherosclerosis in SCAPIS. 12 The few available prospective analyses also reported no associations, but they were likely insufficiently powered (≤254 events). [13] [14] [15] High microbial diversity is generally regarded as beneficial for health, given the low microbial diversity observed in diseased states, such as inflammatory bowel disease. 61 Westernization, often characterized by low fiber and high saturated fat content in the diet, has been associated with lower microbial diversity, with concomitantly reduced microbial capacity to degrade complex carbohydrates, resulting in lower production of short-chain fatty acids, [62] [63] [64] involved in host physiological processes also related to the pathogenesis of ASCVD, such as lipid metabolism and immune system modulation. 2, 65 Antibiotic use, which severely reduces microbial diversity, has also been linked to increased CVD events in a few studies. 66, 67 In the present study, individuals with higher microbial diversity at baseline tend to have healthier lifestyles and better cardiometabolic health compared to those with less diverse gut microbes, consistent with previous cross-sectional studies. 57, 59, 68, 69 The association of gut microbial diversity with the risk of IHD in the present study remained after extensive adjustment of demographic and lifestyle factors, medication use, and prevalent diabetes, known to affect both gut microbiome and ASCVD risk, which suggests that microbial diversity may also affect ASCVD risk through another pathway that is independent of these factors.

text.text: Additional research is needed to elucidate the pathways through which microbial diversity confers protection against ASCVD.
In this study, several taxa are associated with a lower risk of IHD.
SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 belong to the order Christensenellales, whose members have been linked to cardiometabolic health and butyrate-producing capacity.

In a recent study, SFEL01 sp004557245 was identified as having buk, one of the terminal genes for butyrate production from complex polysaccharides, encoding butyrate kinase. 73 Depleted abundance of members of Christensenellales has previously been reported to be associated with higher cardiovascular risk (estimated by CVD risk scores) in individuals without CVD. 13, 60, 74 We further investigated their associations with plasma metabolites, revealing many shared, correlated metabolite associations with species richness.

Strengths of our present analyses include a prospective design, a large sample size, registerbased ascertainment of outcomes, harmonized high-resolution microbiome characterization, and extensive adjustment for confounders, with prioritized species that are robust to variation in data transformation methods.
Firstly, the prospective design substantially reduced the risk of reverse causation compared with previous studies that largely relied on case-control designs.

Secondly, the number of ASCVD events included in this study is by far the largest owing to linkage to national patient and death registers, enabling us to obtain detailed information about diagnoses, hospitalizations, and causes of death, and to reduce the risk of outcome misclassification 80 .

text.text: Third, shotgun metagenomic sequencing and a harmonized bioinformatic pipeline across cohorts enabled species-level resolution.
Previous studies have used low-resolution 16S rRNA data 6, 13, 14 or shallow metagenomic sequencing 15 and thus were only able to report findings at genus level or higher.

text.text: When we adjusted only for demographic and technical variation, as in previous studies, 68 common and 19 rare species were associated with IHD; after further controlling for differences in lifestyle, medication use, and prevalent diabetes, only eight common and one rare species remained.

This underscores the importance of rigorous control of confounding in causal investigations of the microbiome and disease risk, and helps prioritize species for further functional characterization and as potential targets for intervention.
Additionally, the harmonization of confounders appears important when including data from multiple cohorts.

Heterogeneity in associations among most species was substantially reduced in the fully adjusted model, suggesting that after accounting for differences attributable to lifestyle and medications, the associations are more consistent across cohorts.

To note, our model specification assumes that associations of microbial species with ASCVD have a similar confounding structure, which may not hold across all tested microbial species; however, this modeling approach also allows us to test a large number of species and provides greater flexibility in testing our assumptions through multiple sensitivity analyses.

Some studies controlled for differences in BMI statistically or by matching, instead of adjustment for differences in diet or physical activity. 38, 60, 81 However, BMI might also lie in the causal pathway between the gut microbiome and ASCVD, 82, 83 and importantly, adjusting for BMI but not diet or physical activity assumes that the influence of these factors on the gut microbiome and ASCVD risk is solely through BMI modification.

text.text: Nevertheless, our results showed that further adjustments for BMI showed virtually unchanged estimates, likely because diet and physical activity, already adjusted for in the analysis, are strongly correlated with BMI.
Several limitations also need to be considered.
Owing to the observational nature of the study, we cannot offer definitive conclusions regarding the causal relationship between the gut microbiome and ASCVD.
Despite our efforts to control for confounding and the availability of extensive linkage with registers, residual confounding due to measurement errors cannot be ruled out.

We tried to limit this as much as possible, for example, by capturing proton-pump inhibitors use based on their detected metabolites in plasma, as these drugs can be both prescribed and available over the counter.

We also attempted to replicate our findings in external cohorts; however, meta-analyzed estimates from HUNT and FINRISK cohorts showed largely non-replicated associations, except for S. mutans, which was adversely associated with IHD in HUNT participants and was not reliably measured in the shallow-sequenced FINRISK.

While these results suggest that these species may not be truly associated with ASCVD, we cannot rule out methodological differences and the much longer follow-up duration in FINRISK contributing to the non-replication.
The low prevalence of some species might have further limited the statistical power to detect associations.

Inconsistency in published findings remains a concern in microbiome research, 84 partly due to a lack of standardized protocols for sample collection, DNA extraction and sequencing, and bioinformatics pipeline, which can substantially influence the observed microbial composition. [85] [86] [87] Despite these limitations, our study could offer insights on the importance of ensuring sufficient power (i.e., having many events) by including more cohorts, ideally with gut microbiome data processed using a standardized bioinformatic pipeline, and controlling for important covariates such as diet, lifestyle and medication use, in microbiome-disease studies aiming for causal inference.

text.text: In this study, the fecal metagenomic data was only available at baseline, assuming that all microbial species remained stable throughout the follow-up period.
Investigations using repeated measurements of the gut microbiome and atherosclerosis progression would provide stronger evidence of causality between the gut microbiome and ASCVD.
Collectively, our data support the role of the gut microbiome in the pathophysiology of ASCVD.

Our present analysis provides evidence for the protective effect of higher microbial diversity on the long-term risk of ASCVD and shows that low microbial diversity can be present years before the disease occurs, supporting the temporality of the association.

Our data also add to the evidence that gut enrichment of oral taxa S. mutans and L. fermentum, and inflammatory-associated R. gnavus, is likely harmful, while enrichment of two Christensenellales species seems to be protective.
Furthermore, our study identifies several microbial features as targets to prioritize in future studies to confirm their causal roles.
